beginner.headline: Trump Discusses New AI Plans
beginner.brief: US President Donald Trump talked about new plans for artificial intelligence. He wants the US to create an 'AI Force' and appoint an AI leader. Trump said his government will not stop AI from growing. Many people have given warnings about the possible dangers of AI. Trump thinks AI is very important and will be bigger than the Internet. He also said his government would stop bad actors who use AI for wrong things. Some experts say AI development should slow down.

intermediate.headline: Trump Announces 'AI Force' Amid Technology Warnings
intermediate.brief: US President Donald Trump announced he will form an "AI Force" and appoint an artificial intelligence tsar. He stated his administration would not "hinder or stifle the growth" of the industry. This position comes amid warnings about the emergent technology and calls to slow its development until better safeguards are put in place. Many warnings about AI's potential dangers have led to demands for coordinated action on its development. Trump offered no details or a timeline for his plan to create this new "AI Force". He called AI the "next Industrial Revolution," predicting it would be even larger and more impactful. AI is now central to the US-China rivalry as both nations seek to gain an advantage in advanced technology. Researchers have suggested a significant chance that the technology could "endanger humanity". Major AI companies are also developing "super intelligence", which is theoretical technology smarter than humans. Some industry leaders have called for AI development to be regulated, including independent monitoring. However, Sam Altman of OpenAI suggested people should have more faith in AI firms to keep the technology safe.

advanced.headline: Trump Announces 'AI Force' Amid Warnings Over Emergent Technology
advanced.brief: US President Donald Trump has announced plans to establish an "AI Force" and designate an artificial intelligence tsar, despite widespread concerns regarding the emergent technology. He affirmed that his administration would not "in any way hinder or stifle the growth" of the industry, resisting calls for a slowdown to implement better safeguards. Trump did not offer specific details or a timeline for these initiatives. He characterized AI as "the next Industrial Revolution," predicting it could contribute up to 25% of the country's GDP. Furthermore, Trump expressed his desire for the US to maintain its lead over China in artificial intelligence, a key area of their ongoing rivalry. AI development is a central aspect of the US-China rivalry, with both major economies competing for technological superiority. The president also stated his administration would employ existing legal frameworks to address any "bad actors" utilizing AI. He reiterated his view that criticisms and concerns about AI's potential dangers constitute a "hoax." This stance comes as claims from researchers, including one suggesting over a 10% risk of AI "killing all humans," have recently raised alarm bells. Major AI companies are actively racing to develop advanced systems, including theoretical "super intelligence" superior to human intellect. Industry leaders like Anthropic's Dario Amodei have advocated for a deceleration of AI development, proposing industry-wide regulation and independent monitoring. Another co-founder, Jack Clark, suggested that a "kill switch" checked by a third party might become mandatory for the sector. Despite warnings prompting US lawmakers to propose legislation, OpenAI's Sam Altman indicated that Washington struggles to keep pace with regulating the new technology. Altman stated that people should have more faith in AI firms to act responsibly, acknowledging the significant implications. In the UK, Members of Parliament and peers have identified human rights risks from AI, arguing that current laws are ill-equipped to manage its rapid expansion. The Joint Committee on Human Rights has published a report recommending a new AI bill to adequately address these severe threats.
